body.text: Data centre backlash grows as Victorian voters call for major parties to clarify policies
In short:
Community backlash against data centres continues to grow, with the topic now a frequent concern raised by focus groups run by political research group, Redbridge.
Both parties have announced new data centres cannot be built near homes and schools.
But the Coalition has not directly answered questions about whether it will match Labor's pledge to require data centres to provide their own renewable power.

The explosion of data centres — and community backlash against them — has spilled into the state election, with Jess Wilson's Opposition reticent to detail how it will manage the multi-billion dollar industry.
In November 2025, then-Victorian premier Jacinta Allan stood before the Committee for Economic Development of Australia and pledged to make Victoria the country's capital for data centres.
"I want Victoria to be the data centre centre," Ms Allan declared. "We have the land, we have the energy, we have the talent."

Ten months — and a new premier — later, the state government has announced sweeping new data centre regulations, including a ban near homes and schools, as surging community opposition to the resource-hungry projects became impossible to ignore.
Across the state, MPs and candidates have joined community campaigns against the businesses.
"It's gone from zero to 100 in a matter of months," former political strategist and Redbridge Group pollster Kos Samaras told the ABC.
Six months ago, data centres barely rated as a concern for focus groups organised by Redbridge.
Now, they were frequently being raised — unprompted — by voters who demonstrated "extensive awareness" of their size and energy demands.
"By and large, I'd say the [data centre] industry has a lot of social licence work ahead of it, because the community opposition to it is increasing," Samaras observed.
Under the Coalition's plans, data centres will be built in designated precincts away from homes.

But it has been reticent to reveal detailed policies, and did not directly answer questions from the ABC about whether it would match, or better, Labor's proposed sustainability regulations, including that data centres be required to power themselves by providing their own renewable energy supply.

On Saturday, Opposition leader Jess Wilson said the Coalition was open to data centres being powered through gas, despite some experts believing it could take at least five years to develop unproven gas reserves.

"I know Ben Carroll says [data centres] will only be through renewable energy. We are absolutely open to it being through gas as well, because gas is going to be what brings down energy prices here in Victoria but also keeps the lights on," Ms Wilson said.

The ABC, after seeking clarification as to whether that meant tech giants would need to source and fund their own gas supply, was told the exact details were yet to be developed, but the Coalition broadly supported data centres producing more energy than they used.
A spokesperson for Labor said the government introduced "the toughest data centres rules in Australia", while accusing the opposition of not having a plan.
"Liberals don't have a data centre policy — that means they'll let it rip," the spokesperson said.
"Instead of being required to deliver their own renewable energy supply, Jess Wilson would let data centres use up our gas — making your bills way more expensive."
Plumpton fights hyperscale Victorian AI hub

Across Victoria, community groups and local councils are pushing back against the construction of AI data centres, citing concerns about their energy and water use, air and noise pollution, and impact on property valuations.
Some have blamed Labor for fast-tracking approvals of large-scale data centres, and for failing to introduce guardrails earlier.

In Melbourne's north-west, grassroots community organisation Plumpton Action Group was formed in direct response to a proposed hyperscale data centre — the Victorian AI hub — which if built, would span 350 hectares and have a capacity of 2.4 gigawatts.
Co-founder Ella Bourne believes data centres will be a central issue at the ballot box in her local electorate of Sydenham — one of several Labor seats now considered at risk.

A petition calling on the government to fully assess the "environmental, social, cultural and infrastructure implications" of the proposed Victorian AI hub has so far amassed more than 6,000 signatures.
Liberal candidate Nathalie Moussi, One Nation candidate Joh Bauch and even Labor candidate Uros Rasic, have each campaigned against the development.
In Melbourne's west, Labor MP Katie Hall has also opposed the proposed expansion of NextDC's West Footscray, as she faced a challenge from the Greens.

Ms Bourne was highly critical of Labor's controversial Development Facilitation Program (a fast-track planning approvals scheme), the party's proposed 150-metre buffer zone from homes, and the fact that the new regulations would not be apply to projects already being assessed.
However, she would also like to see greater clarity from the Liberal party about its overall plans, saying she supported data centres having to use renewable energy and recycled water.

"I'd like the next government to implement an immediate statewide moratorium until there are proper regulations in place," Ms Bourne said. "Those regulations need to be influenced by proper risk assessments that are independently done."
Local resident and fellow Plumpton Action group member Anthony Stevens said he wanted stronger guardrails from both major parties.
"There needs to be way clearer guidelines and way more open conversation. And it needs to be way less vague," Mr Stevens said.

Last week, the Liberal party also revealed it would wind back the Development Facilitation Program (DFP) "whilst maintaining a pathway for genuinely significant, complex projects of state and economic importance".
The move has been welcomed by Whittlesea council, which had strongly advocated against the scheme because it allowed developers to bypass local councils and apply directly to the Planning Minister.
"Councils and the residents have the best local information," Whittlesea Mayor Lawrie Cox said. "That's been ignored."

When the ABC also sought clarity as to whether that meant councils would be given a say on pending data centre proposals, a Liberal spokesperson said the party would seek independent advice from the Victorian Public Service.

"Should we have the privilege of being elected, the Victorian Public Service will provide advice on the implementation of our policy to ensure data centres are not built in residential areas, adjacent to residential areas, or within the green wedge," a spokesperson said.
There are currently nine data centre projects lodged under the DFP, which Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny declined to make a decision on before the government entered caretaker mode.
Among them are the Victorian AI hub and a proposed data centre in South Morang, which Whittlesea council is fiercely opposed to due to its proximity to homes.
Mr Cox said he also wanted data centres to be held responsible for their impact on the energy supply.
"We don't want blackouts, we don't want impacts like that on the community," Mr Cox said.

No matter which party forms government after the state election, they'll need to contend with the issue of data centres, balancing Victoria's economic needs with the deep unpopularity of the facilities.
The pre-election budget update, published earlier this month, revealed Victoria's economic growth was being "primarily driven by data centre investment".
The Greens have called for a moratorium on all new AI data centres and compensation for affected communities.

One Nation said it would ban new data centres on agricultural land, require environmental assessments and community consultation before approval near homes, and ban retrospective carve-outs for projects already under assessment.

Unlike the US midterms, which saw fierce voter backlash to data centres, Kos Samaras said the parties' policies on data centres in Victoria were unlikely to be a vote driver on their own, in an election dominated by concerns over Big Build corruption, potholes, crime and the cost of living.
But he said concerns about data centres fed into a prevailing perception among many voters that the political class was out of touch.
"It adds to the angst that the electorate has that decision-makers are not actually making decisions for the best interests of the community," Samaras said.
